pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Air Resistance & Friction

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 5 Forces):** Identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction, that act between moving surfaces.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct PE at this band; relates to 3-PS2-1):** Air resistance is not a discrete elementary NGSS performance expectation; the resistive-force idea connects to 3-PS2-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1] an object's motion) and is formalised later under MS-PS2/HS-PS2.

- **Operational details:** At 9-10, air resistance is introduced as a frictional (resistive) force: it acts in the OPPOSITE direction to an object's motion and increases with greater surface area and greater speed. It is best taught through fair-test investigation (parachutes or paper spinners) where children change one variable — usually surface area — and measure fall time with repeat readings. The load-bearing correction is the idea that all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size and shape; this is confronted by discussion then practical test, and connected to real contexts of maximising resistance (parachutes) versus streamlining.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Run a fair-test investigation: vary one variable (parachute/spinner surface area), measure fall time, take repeat readings and compare
Establish air resistance as a force acting OPPOSITE to motion and represent it with an arrow against the direction of travel
Use discuss-then-investigate to confront the 'all objects experience the same air resistance' misconception directly
Anchor in real contexts: parachutes maximise air resistance; streamlined shapes minimise it
Group air resistance with surface friction and water resistance as resistive forces, while distinguishing the medium
keyRepresentations: Arrow pair on a falling object: weight pulling down, air resistance pushing up (opposing motion)
Parachute-size vs fall-time data table and bar chart
commonMisconceptions: All objects experience the same amount of air resistance regardless of size or shape (Oak-named misconception)
Air resistance acts in all directions, or acts downward — it is directional and acts opposite to motion
Air resistance is the same as 'wind'
Mass is irrelevant to falling — yet with air resistance present, two objects of the same shape but different mass do not fall identically
Heavier objects always fall faster (the Aristotelian carryover) — true-ish for same-shape objects in air, but it conflates air resistance with the underlying gravity story

learn.summary: For 9–10 year olds, teach air resistance as a resistive (frictional) force that acts opposite to an object's motion and grows with surface area and speed. The central corrective target is the misconception that all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape. A route well aligned with the curriculum combines a hands-on fair-test investigation using the same sheet of paper flat versus crumpled (so weight is held constant and area becomes the visible cause) with a live falling-object model, in which an upward resistance arrow grows as the object speeds up until it balances weight and the object then falls at a steady speed. Supporting retrieval (ordering by fall time, arrow-direction questions) and a static labelled force diagram serve as scaffolds, not replacements for the predict–measure experience.

activities.title: Growing resistance: drop and watch the arrows balance
feedback: If the learner expects a constant upward push, point to the arrow starting at nothing and growing as speed increases — it depends on how fast the object is moving.
When the arrows balance, name what they see: 'The forces are now balanced, so there's no more speeding up — it falls at a steady speed,' rather than saying it has stopped moving.
In fair-test mode, prompt: 'Only one thing is different between these two — so whatever changed must be causing the different fall.'
activities.rationale: A dynamic model lets children see resistance change with speed and area, which a static picture cannot animate; pairing it with single-variable comparison supports the fair-test reasoning the curriculum expects. The specific advantage of a live simulation over other media is a proposal, not source-established.
sourceClaims: Air resistance is a frictional force that acts opposite to the direction of motion; greater surface area gives more air resistance; the named misconception 'all objects experience the same amount of air resistance, regardless of size or shape' is addressed through discussion and a practical fair-test investigation.
learnerActions: Build a falling object and use a slider to change its surface area — flatten a ball into a flat sheet, or widen a parachute canopy.
Drop it down a tall chute and watch the upward air-resistance arrow grow from nothing as the object speeds up.
Keep watching until the upward arrow matches the downward weight arrow and the object stops speeding up, then falls at a steady speed.

Widen the canopy and observe the arrows balancing sooner, at a lower speed (it floats gently); streamline it and observe the upward arrow growing more slowly, so the object reaches a much higher speed before the arrows balance (it plummets).
Use a 'fair test' mode to drop two objects differing in exactly one variable (e.g. surface area) and read the cause straight off the race.
activities.intendedInsight: Air resistance is not fixed: it grows with both speed and surface area, and always pushes back against the direction of motion. When it balances weight the object stops accelerating and falls at a steady speed (it keeps moving). Two shapes of the same weight are NOT slowed the same.

activities.title: Fair-test investigation: same paper, flat vs crumpled
feedback: If the learner predicts a tie ('same paper, same weight, so same fall'), this is the diagnostic tell — run the flat vs crumpled test and a big vs small parachute with repeat readings to show resistance grows with area.
If the learner says crumpling makes the paper heavier, weigh both: they are identical, so the only change is shape/area and that must be the cause.
Confirm the correct account: 'Both weigh the same, so gravity pulls equally, but the flat sheet has a bigger surface facing the air, so more air resistance pushes up against it and slows it.'
activities.rationale: Holding weight constant while changing only shape removes the 'heavier falls faster' escape route and isolates surface area as the cause, directly confronting the named misconception through predict-then-measure.
sourceClaims: Air resistance is a frictional force that acts opposite to the direction of motion; greater surface area gives more air resistance; the named misconception 'all objects experience the same amount of air resistance, regardless of size or shape' is addressed through discussion and a practical fair-test investigation.
learnerActions: Predict first: drop a flat sheet of paper (held level, not edge-on) and the SAME sheet crumpled into a tight ball together from the same height — which lands first, and why? (Use two identical sheets, one flat and one crumpled, so both can be dropped at once.)
State the prediction and reason aloud or in writing BEFORE dropping.
Drop both and observe which lands first.
Weigh both to confirm they are identical in mass, so weight cannot explain the difference.
Repeat the drop several times and compare; extend to a big vs small parachute, taking repeat readings and recording fall times in a table.
activities.intendedInsight: Because the flat sheet and the crumpled ball are identical paper with the same weight, gravity pulls equally; the flat sheet meets MORE air because of its larger surface area facing the air, so it falls slower. At a given speed, the size of the air resistance depends on surface area and shape, not on the object's weight.

activities.title: Which way does it push? Direction and retrieval practice
feedback: If the learner places air resistance sideways or downward, restate: it acts OPPOSITE to the direction of movement, so upward on something falling; show it on the diagram.
If ordering is wrong, link each shape's area to the size of the air force pushing back on it.
Reinforce that air resistance is a force opposing motion, distinct from a gust of wind.
activities.rationale: Retrieval and direction questions consolidate the arrow direction and the area–fall-time link and surface the common 'same for all shapes' and 'acts in all directions' errors; recognition tasks reinforce but do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning of the investigation.
sourceClaims: Air resistance is a frictional force that acts opposite to the direction of motion; greater surface area gives more air resistance; the named misconception 'all objects experience the same amount of air resistance, regardless of size or shape' is addressed through discussion and a practical fair-test investigation.
learnerActions: Order a set of parachutes/shapes by their fall time.
Answer which way air resistance pushes on a falling object — up, down, or sideways — and justify it.
Use a slider to explore how changing surface area changes fall time, predicting before each change.
Draw or complete a force diagram on a falling object showing weight down and air resistance opposing the motion (up for a falling object).
activities.intendedInsight: Air resistance acts opposite to the direction of movement — upward on a falling object — and larger area gives more resistance and a slower fall. It is not 'wind' and does not act in all directions.

activities.title: Connecting the ideas: parachutes, streamlining, water and the Moon
feedback: If the learner attributes the parachute slowdown to weight, point back to the canopy: the weight is unchanged, the area increased.
If the learner expects different fall times on the Moon, remind them air resistance needs air; with none, only gravity acts and the two papers land together.
Accept and build on valid water-resistance examples (e.g. swimming, a boat's shape), linking the size of the force to area and speed.
activities.rationale: Transfer to real contexts and the airless case checks whether the learner has generalised the resistive-force idea rather than memorised the paper result, and separates air resistance from the underlying gravity story. The water-resistance and Moon material is inherited from the row's objective and probes and is a research-informed proposal, not source-verified.
learnerActions: Explain what a parachutist changes to slow down (area, not weight) when a big canopy opens.
Contrast maximising air resistance (parachutes) with minimising it (streamlined shapes).

Give an everyday example of water resistance and explain how it, like air resistance and surface friction, opposes motion; water and air resistance act on objects moving through water or air, while surface friction acts between surfaces in contact.
Predict what the flat sheet and the crumpled ball would do if dropped where there is no air at all (e.g. the Moon) and explain why.
activities.intendedInsight: Air resistance, water resistance and surface friction are all resistive forces that oppose motion. Air and water resistance can be increased (bigger area facing the air or water) or reduced (streamlining); surface friction depends mainly on how rough the surfaces are and how hard they press together. Without air (as on the Moon) there is no air resistance, so the paper ball and the flat sheet would land together.

constraints: Fair tests must change exactly one variable at a time (e.g. surface area) and take repeat readings before comparing fall times.
Hold weight constant (same sheet flat vs crumpled) when isolating surface area, so learners cannot explain the result by weight.
Describe balanced forces carefully: at terminal velocity the object stops speeding up and falls at a steady speed — it has NOT stopped moving. Balanced forces mean no acceleration, not rest.
Air resistance acts opposite to motion (upward on a falling object), not in all directions and not simply 'downward'; it is not the same as wind.
Air resistance requires air: in the airless case (Moon) there is no air resistance, so the same-weight objects land together regardless of shape.
Static force diagrams are a useful reference but cannot animate resistance growing with speed; use them as scaffolds alongside a dynamic model or practical test.
Recognition and ordering tasks reinforce and reveal misconceptions but do not by themselves elicit the independent predict-then-measure reasoning; pair them with the investigation.

The claim that mass affects falling when air resistance is present (same-shape objects of different mass need not reach the same terminal speed) is an advanced nuance; introduce only if it does not reintroduce 'heavier falls faster' as a blanket rule, and keep it separate from the surface-area message for this age band.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The dynamic/live-model advantage over static or quiz formats is presented as a proposal; no source establishes it is necessary or superior for a given learner.

The source lists 'heavier objects always fall faster (Aristotelian carryover)' as a misconception but also notes it is 'true-ish for same-shape objects in air'. With air resistance, a heavier same-shape object can reach a higher terminal speed. To avoid reintroducing a wrong blanket rule for 9–10s, activities keep the primary message as 'surface area (and speed), not weight, changes air resistance' and treat mass effects as an optional advanced nuance.
The second source (mass affects falling with air resistance) is marked verified:false in the row; its claim is presented only as an advanced nuance and not used to drive the core activities.

Original artefact-fit text asserted the balance relationship is 'only a live sim makes felt' and that a fixed quiz/static image 'cannot' teach the dynamic balance, and that 3D 'adds nothing' / dialogue 'cannot deliver' the investigation. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the source and have been softened to scaffold/affordance statements.

The original terminal-velocity description ('object stops accelerating', 'falls at a steady speed') is physically sound and preserved; the constraint and feedback explicitly clarify the object keeps moving, to prevent a 'balanced = stopped' misreading.

Activity 4's water-resistance examples and the resistive-force grouping with the airless (Moon) case are inherited from the row's objective and probe questions, not from the cited source (which concerns air resistance only); its sourceClaims is therefore [] and the material is flagged as an unvalidated proposal.

The Moon statement is scoped to the same-weight paper scenario; in a true vacuum all objects regardless of mass fall together, but the narrower scenario-bound wording is retained to match the activity's task.

The objective's 'surface texture'/surface-friction strand is only lightly touched; emphasis follows the original row's air-resistance focus and could be extended if friction between solid surfaces is required.

assess.poeTask: Drop a flat sheet of paper and the SAME sheet crumpled into a ball, together, from the same height. Ask the child to predict which lands first and WHY before dropping. Predicting a tie ('same paper, same weight') is the diagnostic tell; the crumpled ball clearly winning — with weight held constant — pins the cause on air resistance and surface area, not weight.
probeDeeper: A parachutist opens a big parachute and slows down. What changed to give more air resistance — the weight or the area?
Which way does air resistance push on the falling paper — up, down, or sideways? Why?
Would air resistance matter if there were no air at all, like on the Moon? What would the two papers do then?
Is water resistance like air resistance? Give an example.
assess.correctAnswer: The screwed-up ball lands first. Both weigh the same, so gravity pulls equally, but the flat sheet has a much bigger surface facing the air, so it meets MORE air resistance pushing up against its fall — that slows it. Air resistance depends on surface area (and speed), not on weight; the ball has less area, so less air resistance.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'They'll land together — air pushes the same on everything, whatever the shape.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fair-test flat vs crumpled (same paper), and a big vs small parachute, with repeat readings; air resistance grows with area.
errorPatterns.distractor: They land at the same time — air resistance is the same on everything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a tie, or can't link shape to the size of the air force.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The crumpled one is heavier now — that's why it falls faster.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh both — they're identical; the only change is shape/area, so air resistance must be the cause.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says screwing the paper up makes it heavier.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Air resistance pushes in all directions, or downwards too.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Air resistance acts OPPOSITE to the direction of movement — upwards on a falling object; show it on the force diagram.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or says air resistance acting sideways or downward, not opposite the motion.

responseLevels.gap: Predicts they land together (air resistance the same on all) or says the crumpled paper is heavier; puts air resistance in the wrong direction.
responseLevels.full: Explains air/water resistance and friction as forces that oppose motion whose size grows with surface area (and speed), so the flat sheet with more area falls slower than the identical-weight ball — transferring to parachutes and to the Moon (no air -> land together).
responseLevels.partial: Knows air resistance slows things and can give examples, but explains the paper result by weight, or lists the resistive forces without linking the size of the force to surface area/speed and its opposing direction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I drop a flat sheet of paper and, at the same moment, the SAME sheet screwed into a tight ball, from the same height. Which lands first — and why, given they're made of exactly the same paper and weigh the same?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the two are the same paper and the same weight, the child can't fall back on 'the heavier one'. A child who understands air resistance attributes the difference to the flat sheet's larger area meeting more air. A child holding the Oak misconception — 'air resistance is the same on everything regardless of shape/size' — predicts a tie or says the flat one is 'lighter'. Tier 2 forces area (not weight) as the cause.

sources.source: Oak National Academy — Air resistance (KS2 lesson plan)

sources.claim: With air resistance present, mass affects falling (objects of the same shape but different mass do not reach the same terminal speed), nuancing the simple 'all objects fall at the same rate' rule.
